title: Your head is older than your feet

beats.vo: Your head is older than your feet.
beats.visual: Ink figure standing side-on on paper grid. Two small ink clocks: one at the head, one at the feet. Head clock's second hand visibly runs ahead. Must read in under 2 s.

beats.vo: Every second you're standing, it pulls a tiny bit further ahead.
beats.visual: Mono counter beside the head clock ticking up in tiny increments. Camera: straight push-in (z) toward the head clock, motivated by the counter.

beats.vo: Here's the thing. Gravity doesn't just pull on you. It slows down time.
beats.visual: Earth drawn as a wide ink arc at the bottom. Ink gravity arrows point down. The graph-paper grid compresses toward the ground (lines bunch closer near Earth) = time running slower.

beats.vo: The closer you are to Earth, the slower your clock ticks.
beats.visual: A vertical column of 4 identical clocks at rising heights; hands sweep at visibly rising speed with height. Small Graphite label 'speeds exaggerated'. Camera: straight tilt up the column (y).

beats.vo: Your feet are closer. Your head is higher. So your head's time runs a little faster.
beats.visual: Back to the figure. Camera travels straight up (y) from the feet clock to the head clock as each is named. Red underline under 'faster' caption.

beats.vo: Sounds made up. So in 2010, physicists at a U.S. lab called NIST tested it.
beats.visual: Mono date stamp '2010 · NIST' slams in like a rubber stamp. Lab bench drawn line by line.

beats.vo: They took two super-precise atomic clocks, and raised one by about a foot. Two steps up a staircase.
beats.visual: Two clocks side by side on the bench. A two-step staircase draws in; one clock climbs the two steps. Dimension line with arrowheads labelled '33 cm ≈ 1 ft' in mono.
Tick marks spray out of the higher clock slightly quicker than the lower. Red underline. Hold still ~1 s.

beats.vo: Over a whole seventy-nine year life, those two steps add up to about ninety billionths of a second.
beats.visual: A long ink timeline labelled '79 years' runs across the frame; at its end a tiny gap labelled in mono '≈ 0.000 000 09 s'. Camera: straight push-in (z) on the tiny gap.

beats.vo: Far too small to feel. But real.
beats.visual: The gap shrinks to a single ink dot. Marker highlight behind 'real'.

beats.vo: And your phone feels it. GPS satellites fly high, so their clocks run fast.
beats.visual: Camera pulls straight back (z) then rises (y): Earth arc small at bottom, an ink-drawn GPS satellite high on a dashed path, with its own clock running fast. Still paper and ink, no black space.

beats.vo: So engineers set them slower on the ground, before launch. Without that fix, your map would be wrong.
beats.visual: The satellite clock on a ground bench; an ink hand turns its knob back. Cut to a simple street-grid map with a pin: pin drifts off the street (dashed), then snaps back onto it.

beats.vo: The verdict? True. The higher you are, the faster your time runs.
screen: The higher you are, the faster your time runs.
beats.visual: Signature: 'CASE FILE 001' header, a big Anton 'TRUE' stamp slams in Horizon orange on 'True', the rule line below in Barlow. Hold 1 s of stillness.

beats.vo: So next time you take the stairs, you just aged a little faster. Barely.
beats.visual: Figure climbs a staircase; a tiny '+' tick pops at each step.

beats.vo: Which means your head really is older than your feet. By a hair.
beats.visual: Back to the opening framing: figure with head and feet clocks. A single ink hair springs up on the head on 'By a hair'. End on the rule card for ~1 s.

end_card.text: Case file 001 · TRUE · The higher you are, the faster your time runs.
